questions: Does the subgraph have to be an induced subgraph of T, or may we select any subset of edges that still forms a tree with the required degree conditions?
When selecting the subgraph, are we allowed to delete vertices without also deleting all incident edges, i.e., can isolated vertices appear in the subgraph?
Must the subgraph remain connected (i.e., be a single tree), or can it consist of multiple disconnected components that each satisfy the degree conditions?
If the original tree T contains vertices of degree other than 1 or 4, are we allowed to use those vertices in the subgraph after removing some of their incident edges to reduce their degree?
In the case that multiple subgraphs achieve the maximum size, is any such size acceptable, or must we output additional information (e.g., the number of such subgraphs)?
Are there any constraints on the size of the alkane subgraph besides having at least one vertex of degree 4 (e.g., must it contain at least one leaf vertex of degree 1)?
Should the output be the number of vertices in the alkane subgraph, or the number of vertices plus the number of edges (i.e., the total size of the subgraph)?
Are there any special handling rules for the case N = 1 (a single vertex tree) or N = 2, where no vertex can have degree 4?
answers: Not specified beyond what's given; assume the subgraph must be induced, i.e. contain all edges of T between the selected vertices.
Not specified beyond what's given; every selected vertex must have degree exactly 1 or 4 within the subgraph, so isolated vertices are not allowed.
Not specified beyond what's given; assume the subgraph must remain a single connected tree, as implied by the alkane definition.
Not specified beyond what's given; a vertex's degree in the subgraph is determined only by which incident edges are selected, regardless of its degree in T.
Not specified beyond what's given; any subgraph satisfying the degree conditions is acceptable, regardless of tie count.
Not specified beyond what's given; the alkane definition only requires degree 1 or 4 for every vertex and at least one degree-4 vertex, with no additional leaf requirement stated.
The output should be the number of vertices in the alkane subgraph, as stated in the Output section.
Since N can be 1 or 2, no degree-4 vertex can exist in those cases, so the answer would simply be -1; no special-case handling beyond the general rule is needed.
inline_prompts: You are given an undirected tree T with N vertices, numbered 1, 2, \ldots, N. The i-th edge is an undirected edge connecting vertices A_i and B_i. A graph is defined to be an alkane if and only if it satisfies the following conditions: - The graph is an undirected tree. - Every vertex has degree 1 or 4, and there is at least one vertex of degree 4. Note that the subgraph must be induced, i.e. contain all edges of T between the selected vertices. Determine whether there exists a subgraph of T that is an alkane, and if so, find the maximum number of vertices in such a subgraph. Input The input is given from Standard Input in the following format: N A_1 B_1 A_2 B_2 \vdots A_{N - 1} B_{N - 1} Output If there exists a subgraph of T that is an alkane, print the maximum number of vertices in such a subgraph. Otherwise, print -1. Constraints - 1 \leq N \leq 2 \times 10^5 - 1 \leq A_i, B_i \leq N - All input values are integers.
